work.title: Homily on Lazarus raised after four days II

paragraphs.text: A discourse by our holy father John Chrysostom on Lazarus, who had been dead for four days. Just as a loving mother, having offered her breast to her infant, rejoices as the child draws in the gentle nourishment of milk, but then, when the milk sets and curdles, blocking the passage through the breast, the child cries and the mother suffers, being accustomed to feeding her child, yet seeing that no nourishment is being supplied, so we too, having offered the first breast to your minds, rejoiced as you sucked the milk of words. Then, when a cloud of forgetfulness came over the mind and stopped the discourse, you became angry, as though deprived of an understanding of the Gospel teachings. And we were distressed, striving to understand how this had happened to us, so that we might learn that it depends neither on the one who wills, nor on the one who runs, nor on the one who strives, but on God who shows mercy. Therefore, since God gives speakers their gift, not according to the speakers’ authority, but because of the listeners’ need, let us pray to him and, from what has been read to us today— the Gospel teachings—let us draw the water of instruction according to our capacity to drink. “There was a certain man who was ill, Lazarus,” it says, “from Bethany, from the village of Mary

and Martha her sister. It was Mary who had anointed the Lord with ointment, whose brother Lazarus was ill.” Jesus said, “This illness is not for death, but for the glory of God, so that God may be glorified through it.” Returning to this, I say: “This illness is not for death, but for the glory of God.” It is not an illness, but a strengthening. O illness, physician to the sick, guide to faith, adversary of death, opponent of the devil, beginning of salvation! O illness, the soul’s indestructible root, teacher of faith, provision for godliness! O illness, driving fires from the soul, sprinkling the sweat of baptism, and weaving bright garments for the soul! O illness, giver of heavenly bread, pure lamp of faith, snare for the devil, and a sign for mankind! “When Jesus heard,” it says, “he remained for two days in the place where he was.” What need, then, was there for the Lord to remain after hearing this, rather than going at once to the sick man? He was waiting for Lazarus’s death, so that through his death he might, by miracles, demonstrate greater faith to those who saw. Afterward Jesus said to his disciples, “Lazarus our friend has fallen asleep, but I am going to wake him.” For truly, human death It seems to be sleep, O Lord. “I am going to wake him.” Are you saying that, if you are here, you cannot bring the dead man to life?

But even so the Jews will not receive grace if I am not there. Instead, when he rises, they may begin to think that Lazarus came to life through some chance occurrence. But I myself am coming, so that when I arrive they may be eyewitnesses of the miracles performed by me, and, having received grace from me, they may come to firm faith. “Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I am going to wake him.” And when the disciples heard this, they said, “If he has fallen asleep, he will recover.” They answered not so much from devotion to God as from medical knowledge. For sleep, in those who are unconscious, does harm when prolonged; afterward it brings [?] to those burning with fire. Since the disciples thought that the Lord was speaking about resting in sleep, he said plainly, “Lazarus has died. And for your sake I rejoice that I was not there, so that you may believe. But let us go to him.” You who do not desire the death of sinners, do you rejoice at the death of a friend? Yes, I rejoice, not for my own sake or for the sake of the man who died, but for your sake. For I wish to take death as a foundation for your faith. O death, a joy to Christ! O death, full of life! O death, deliverer from death, beginning of salvation, a rising for the fallen, rest for the suffering, healing for the sick, for the righteous

relief, destruction for the devil, cleansing for demons, renewal for Adam, the first to be created, an aid to joy! But to shorten my account, let me say: he went to Bethany. Lazarus’s two sisters met him. They fell at the Lord’s feet, weeping and saying, “Lord, if you had been here, our brother would not have died.” Was he not there, then? He was not there in body, but in his divinity he was not only there but also in heaven. For how did he know when Lazarus died? Through the invisible power of his divinity. And they said, “Lord, if you had been here, our brother would not have died.” And the Lord said to them, “Believe, and you will see the glory of God,” teaching that faith is a helper in good works. And when he saw them weeping, and the Jews who had come [?], he became angry in spirit and troubled himself, and said, “Where have you laid him?” What does “in spirit” mean? Wait, beloved, and shortly you will find the answer to what you seek. He troubled himself, not as we are troubled by fear. or be troubled by sorrow. But he troubled himself and said, “Where have you laid him?” Do you think he did not know where he was buried? He who knew when he died! But he combines human words with divine miracles, to show that he was also a man,

as the prophet also says: “He is a man, and who will understand him?” He commanded this to signify that he is also something else, namely God. “Where have you laid him?” And Mary said, “Come and see, Lord.” And Jesus shed tears. Why did he need to shed tears for someone whom he was about to raise shortly? But Jesus shed tears to teach compassion—weeping with those who weep—by deed rather than by word. Jesus shed tears, but did not weep uncontrollably. For he rejects shedding no tears at all as hardness and lack of compassion, while correcting excessive weeping as weak and unmanly. But setting a limit to compassion, he shed tears. He goes to the cave and sees a stone lying over the tomb. He commanded the Jews standing there to roll away the stone. You who say, “If you have faith like a grain, you will say to this mountain, ‘Rise and throw yourself into the sea,’ and it will be so for you”—how is it that now you yourself cannot roll away the stone? “But I do this not because I cannot,” he said, “but so that they may not think that what is being done is an illusion. I command the Jews themselves to roll away the stone with their hands, reserving the greater miracle for myself, so that they themselves may be witnesses to the miracles done by me.” Then, after the stone had been rolled away, he looked up to heaven and said, “Father, I thank you that you have heard me.” But when did he pray?

Now receive, beloved, the explanation of the saying that you were seeking a little earlier. For when he was angered in spirit, then he also prayed. And having said this, he cried out in a loud voice, saying, “Lazarus, come out!” And immediately the dead man came out, his hands and feet bound with strips of cloth. O power of the voice, which overturned Hades, shattered the bronze gates, broke the iron bars, and raised the dead man! O power of the voice, which gathered the separated limbs together and set him upright, and brought what did not exist into being! Beloved, direct your mind to this voice, and you will find the very same word that was spoken at the creation of the world: “Let there be light,” and there was light. “Let there be stars in the firmament of heaven,” and they came to be. “Lazarus, come out!” And the bodily strength that had drained away filled his limbs again. “Lazarus, come out!” And the dead man arose and became like those who had not died. “Lazarus, come out!” And his soul was drawn out from the depths of the earth. Neither the devil speaking against it nor death standing in its way prevented it; rather, rejoicing, it recognized its own body. Beloved, having seen God's work in these wondrous deeds, do not reject the resurrection or disbelieve in it. Let Lazarus be your [?], and in him yourself

having seen, believe in the resurrection. For the same voice will raise us all. As the apostle also says somewhere: “For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise without decay.” By the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and power, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
